chapter: American Jazz Orchestra, conducting and teaching
title: Conducting in Cologne, Smithsonian Jazz Orchestra, Ellington scores, New School start
summary: Conducting the WDR orchestra, substituting for the Smithsonian orchestra, transcribing Ellington scores, and starting at the New School.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: would conduct when John wasn’t there. Then Mel Lewis had been working for years with what they call the Westdeutscher Rundfunk, which is the radio orchestra in Cologne Germany. And he got me on that. So for two summers I conducted that orchestra in Cologne. Did the “Rhapsody in Blue” and there’s a funny story about that with Gunther Schuller. And the “Rhapsody in Blue” and the Paul Whiteman program with the full arrangements for the strings and all this kind of stuff. And did another concert with Milt Grayson who had sung with Duke Ellington’s band, and Lynn Roberts. And then another repertory band started called the Smithsonian Jazz Orchestra. And the conductors of that were Gunther Schuller and David Baker. And I was hired originally to be the contractor, to be the tenor soloist and to be kind of like the third conductor. That didn’t really happen. I wound up becoming the substitute conductor, when Gunther or David couldn’t make it. And that band lasted a long — that band is still going but my days in it were about maybe ten years or so. And there I got to meet a whole nother tranche of sorry — another tranche of big band veterans and people that weren’t in New York who I didn’t get to know, and there were all these other wonderful musicians. So at that point I started to lose the impetus after ten or fifteen years of having my own big band and of copying all those parts. I mean I used to, before Jazz at Lincoln Center started all that stuff, I mean I still have a dent in my finger, a guy named Mark Tucker, who was a wonderful Ellington scholar. He edited the Ellington Reader. He was the one who prepared the Ellington big band, the Ellington musical library that eventually went to the Smithsonian, that is now, John Hasse got it at the Smithsonian. And he gave me Xeroxed copies of, I mean a file cabinet’s worth of handwritten Ellington scores. So I started transcribing those for my band, which was a great lesson. And I’m trying to get my — with this finger right here — with the old pencil and the old thing, and even with my students now when I have them do kind of writing assignments, I kind of insist, as much as I can, that they do it by hand. I mean all the computer, that’s great and that’s what they’re going to do. But you are going to write out this Ellington thing by hand, the third alto part, looking at the concert score and saying okay it’s G sharp and all that kind of stuff. Because you learn so much more. So I started having, I stopped having like the impetus to have my own band. Plus I was teaching, I started teaching at the New School in 19— well I worked with Sylvia Sims, a great singer, and her trio was Fred Hirsch and Steve Wispina and myself. And Fred was teaching at the New School. This would have been around 1990. And he said man, would you like to fill in and sub, I can’t make it. I said well what’s the class? Well some kind of like styles analysis, but you can do whatever the hell you want. So I went in and I really enjoyed it. And so I called Fred back and I said would you mind if I call up Martin Mueller, the head of the program, and like pitched my soul for a class? But I said only if you say okay. He said I don’t care, I’m going to leave there anyway. But
